intro: The ball has its own tune, triple pulse and glittering harp writing. The idée fixe enters that social world without abolishing it: the beloved’s melody bends to the waltz. Compare the long middle recollection with the much shorter glimpse near the end.
question: Can a private obsession keep time with a public dance?

cues.title: A room taking shape
cues.text: The opening prepares the ball before presenting its main waltz tune. The score combines trembling strings with rising harp figures. Listen for the sound gathering into a dance rather than beginning with a fully formed melody.
cues.evidence: Score, opening bars, shows string tremolo and staggered harp entries. Report: level rises from −22.4 dB at 0:05 to −6.9 dB at 0:25; instrument identities come from the score.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Find the first beat
cues.text: After the introductory surge, a quieter dance takes over. Try feeling one strong beat followed by two lighter ones, then listen to how the melody crosses that pattern. The waltz’s regular footing will remain important when the idée fixe appears.
cues.evidence: Score, main waltz after the introduction; report drops from −9.9 dB at 0:30 to −27.5 dB at 0:35. Placement is approximate, not beat-aligned.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A ball inside a symphony
cues.text: Berlioz’s programme places the artist amid the bustle of a festive gathering. A waltz therefore does more than supply light relief between large movements: it gives the recurring melody a public setting in which a private thought can intrude.
cues.evidence: Berlioz’s published programme, movement II, describes the festive gathering and the beloved’s recurring image.

cues.title: Prepare to compare melodies
cues.text: Keep the waltz tune in mind as this first large dance span approaches a quieter turn. Its melody and the idée fixe are different material. The connection between them will be the continuing dance pulse, not an identical tune.
cues.evidence: Score contrasts the waltz material with the idée fixe at bars 120–162. Report shows a substantial level drop and a structural boundary around 1:58–2:00.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The idée fixe dances
cues.text: In this central passage, the beloved’s melody fits the waltz’s triple time. Listen for a longer, searching line against the dance accompaniment. Recognition does not require the first movement’s tempo or scoring: the melodic shape survives its new setting.
cues.evidence: Score commentary identifies bars 120–162 as the central idée fixe. Report: the contrasting quieter region begins around 2:00 and continues through 2:40; the theme identification is score-based.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Revised in Florence
cues.text: Berlioz did not leave the ball as he first wrote it. In Florence in April 1831 he reworked its orchestration and supplied a new coda. The glitter and momentum belong to a score shaped after the Paris premiere, not to one untouched burst of inspiration.
cues.evidence: Hector Berlioz Website, score commentary, cites the April 1831 Florence revision and new coda.

cues.title: The dance reclaims the room
cues.text: The returning waltz is more than a repeat of the opening’s mood. After the idée fixe, the same dance material has a different dramatic meaning: the gathering continues, while the listener knows what has interrupted the artist’s attention.
cues.evidence: Score shows the return of waltz material after the central idée fixe. Report: level and brightness increase around 3:00–3:20, locating the larger return region.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Weight without a march
cues.text: The dance grows stronger without losing its triple-time character. Follow the pulse through the fuller sound. Increased orchestral weight does not turn this movement into the square tread of the execution march that will come later.
cues.evidence: Report: stronger windows around 4:00–4:20 include −6.3 dB at 4:15. Triple metre and the contrast with movement IV are established by the score.

cues.title: Two written harp parts
cues.text: The score gives the ball two separate harp parts, unlike the surrounding movements. Their interlocking figures help define the setting. Two parts do not by themselves tell us how many players were used in this recording; no session seating plan has been identified.
cues.evidence: Orchestral score, movement II, two harp staves. The recording sources identify the orchestra but do not document the harp personnel.

cues.title: One last private glimpse
cues.text: Near the end, the idée fixe returns briefly rather than reclaiming its full central span. Listen for the scale of the interruption: a remembered fragment can suspend the dance’s momentum without establishing another large episode.
cues.evidence: Score commentary identifies the abbreviated return at bars 302–319. Report: the strong passage at 4:55 gives way to restrained windows at 5:05–5:25, before the next surge.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The ballroom closes
cues.text: The final rush replaces the brief recollection with the dance’s outward energy. Compare the force of this ending with the first movement’s quiet resolution. The symphony can close a movement decisively while leaving its recurring thought unresolved.
cues.evidence: Report: level rises from −26.8 dB at 5:25 to −7.5 dB at 5:30 and stays strong through 5:55, before the final decay.

transitions.title: The swell becomes a dance
transitions.how: The introductory swell releases into a quieter, clearly shaped waltz. Trembling and rising figures have prepared the space; the tune now makes the triple pulse easy to follow.
transitions.evidence: Score, opening and main waltz; report: −9.9 dB at 0:30 drops to −27.5 dB at 0:35.

transitions.title: The beloved enters the metre
transitions.how: The orchestral surface withdraws, but the dance’s pulse continues. The idée fixe enters a metre already established by other material: Berlioz changes the melody’s surroundings instead of stopping the ball for an unrelated slow episode.
transitions.evidence: Score, bars 120–162; report boundary at 1:58 and level drop of about 15 dB from 1:55 to 2:00.

transitions.title: The dance returns
transitions.how: The central recollection gives way to the waltz material. Renewed orchestral strength makes the return audible without changing the basic dance metre. Compare the tune with its first presentation, not just the volume.
transitions.evidence: Score, return after the idée fixe; report changes at 2:46 and 3:00, followed by stronger A-major windows around 3:05–3:20. Key estimates corroborate the score only.

transitions.title: Momentum briefly suspended
transitions.how: A stronger closing drive withdraws into a compressed recollection of the idée fixe. The interruption is shorter than the central episode, so memory now works as a fleeting glimpse rather than a new large section.
transitions.evidence: Score, bars 302–319; report falls from −5.4 dB at 4:55 to about −26 dB at 5:05–5:15.

transitions.title: The dance sweeps onwards
transitions.how: The recollection yields to a forceful final rush. The coda does not reconcile the two melodies; it restores the ballroom’s momentum and brings this movement to a brilliant stop.
transitions.evidence: Score, coda after the brief idée fixe; report boundary at 5:28 and rise of about 19 dB between 5:25 and 5:30.

Critic for the Journal des débats; Conservatoire librarian; touring conductor
Shakespeare, Goethe and Virgil supplied the subjects of his largest works
Four symphonies; operas; dramatic and sacred choral works; songs; an orchestration treatise
composer.background:
Berlioz grew up in La Côte-Saint-André, between Lyon and Grenoble, in the household of a physician who taught him Latin and expected him to study medicine. He learned flute and guitar, but never acquired the pianist’s routine of composing at a keyboard. Virgil’s account of Dido’s death affected him as a schoolboy; forty years later he would set it in Les Troyens. Sent to Paris in 1821, he attended anatomy lectures while spending his evenings at the Opéra. The theatre’s performances of Gluck offered a different education: declamation, orchestral gesture and the pacing of a dramatic scene.

He abandoned medicine, studied with Jean-François Le Sueur and entered the Conservatoire in 1826. His first large works included a Messe solennelle and the unfinished opera Les Francs-juges, whose overture survived independently. The Prix de Rome required a prescribed cantata; Berlioz finally won it in 1830, on his fourth attempt. The prize sent him to the Villa Medici, but the decisive musical experiences had already happened in Paris. Conservatoire performances under François-Antoine Habeneck introduced him to Beethoven’s symphonies, while an English theatrical company introduced him to Shakespeare.
composer.epithet: He made orchestral colour, the position of a sound in space, and the return of a remembered melody into structural events.
